paragraphs: Separating an object from a video becomes harder when its shadow, reflection, and other visual effects should move with it. These effects depend on scene geometry and lighting, and reliable labels can be difficult to collect. This paper learns the separation without such labels, starting from a rough object mask and predicting an image layer together with its transparency.

Simply requiring the layers to reconstruct the video leaves many possible answers. The authors address this ambiguity using a coordination game: each network predicts one object's effects without seeing the other networks' decisions. The rules encourage mutually compatible choices, making the intended decomposition a focal point around which the predictions can agree. The network learns by playing this game with itself.

The training combines reconstruction and sparsity objectives. The authors demonstrate direct, feed-forward predictions on a challenging synthetic dataset and report that pretraining on it substantially reduces optimization time for real videos. The contribution is a way to guide ambiguous decomposition through coordinated predictions.
neurips-2022-associating-objects-and-the.tldr: A self-supervised coordination game teaches networks to separate video objects together with their associated shadows, reflections, and other effects.

paragraphs: Graph outlier detection asks which nodes look unusual given their connections and attributes. Although many algorithms address this problem, comparing them has been difficult without a shared evaluation framework. BOND supplies a comprehensive benchmark for unsupervised detection on static graphs with node attributes, helping organize evidence about which approaches work well under different conditions.

The benchmark compares 14 methods, spanning classical matrix factorization and graph neural networks. It uses nine real datasets and evaluates two major kinds of artificially introduced outliers separately from naturally occurring outliers. This distinction matters because performance on constructed anomalies and performance on real anomalies answer different questions about a detector's usefulness.

BOND also generates graphs of different sizes using an existing random graph technique. These datasets support comparisons of running time and memory consumption alongside detection performance. The authors use the experiments to discuss existing methods' strengths, weaknesses, and research opportunities. Freely available, extensible code makes the evaluation framework a resource for further comparisons rather than a single algorithm proposal.
neurips-2022-bond-benchmarking-unsupervi.tldr: BOND compares 14 graph outlier detectors across detection settings and computational costs in a shared, extensible benchmark.

paragraphs: Optical Chemical Structure Recognition converts pictures of chemical compounds into molecular structures that software can process. Traditional systems detect entities such as atoms and bonds before assembling the structure. More recent neural systems approach the task like image captioning, but the paper identifies their heavy demand for training examples as a motivation for revisiting explicit detection and reconstruction.

CEDe provides expert-curated annotations for chemical images drawn from scientific literature datasets. Its annotations include more than 700,000 bounding boxes around chemical entities, together with information needed to reconstruct molecular structures. This gives researchers supervision for the intermediate recognition steps, rather than only the final molecular description.

The authors also release a synthetic dataset containing one million molecular images and annotations to support investigation of transfer learning under limited real-data availability. Their benchmarks show that detection-and-reconstruction models can match or exceed captioning-style models while using 100 times fewer training examples. The result supports this structured approach as a potentially more data-efficient route to recognizing chemical diagrams.
neurips-2022-cede-a-collection-of-expert.tldr: CEDe supplies expert chemical-image annotations and benchmarks showing that explicit detection and reconstruction can greatly reduce training-data requirements.

paragraphs: Continual learning must balance remembering earlier tasks with adapting to new ones. The paper calls these goals stability and plasticity. When past training data is no longer available in full, deciding how much influence individual examples should have becomes especially valuable: an example's contribution to new learning may differ from its contribution to retaining earlier knowledge.

The authors study these contributions by slightly changing an example's weight and examining the resulting influence. Conventional influence-function calculations involve an inverse Hessian, which is burdensome for neural networks. Their MetaSP algorithm simulates two key steps of that calculation to estimate influence separately for stability and plasticity without that storage and computation burden.

MetaSP then combines the two influence estimates through a dual-objective optimization aimed toward Pareto optimality, balancing the competing goals. The combined influence guides both model updates and the selection of examples stored for rehearsal. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on task-incremental and class-incremental benchmarks, supporting example influence as a useful control signal for continual learning.
neurips-2022-exploring-example-influence.tldr: MetaSP estimates how examples affect remembering and adaptation, then combines those estimates to guide continual learning and rehearsal.

paragraphs: The Weisfeiler-Lehman test is a reference point for understanding how graph neural networks distinguish graph structures. Earlier work established that graph neural networks can simulate this test, connecting their expressive power to a well-studied graph procedure. However, the known simulations could require large neural networks at each node and feature vectors whose length grew linearly with the graph's node count.

This paper gives a substantially more compact simulation. For a graph with n nodes, the network implementing each node's combination function uses only a number of parameters polynomial in log n. The feature information exchanged between nodes requires only O(log n) bits. These bounds sharply reduce the resources needed by the earlier constructions.

The authors also establish logarithmic lower bounds for feature length and neural-network size. These show that the construction is near optimal in the stated complexity measures. The result strengthens the expressiveness connection by demonstrating that simulating the test need not carry the large representation and parameter costs of previous simulations.
neurips-2022-exponentially-improving-the.tldr: A compact graph neural network construction simulates the Weisfeiler-Lehman test with polylogarithmic parameters and logarithmic-bit node features.

paragraphs: Standard diffusion generators end their sampling process at a predetermined time. First Hitting Diffusion Models instead stop at a random first hitting time, allowing the stopping point to depend on the individual sample. The paper uses this change to extend diffusion generation across continuous data and a range of discrete or structured domains.

Training follows a maximum-likelihood approach built around diffusion trajectories augmented from observed data. These trajectories use conditional first hitting processes, or bridges, derived through Doob's h-transform. This provides a different construction from the time-reversal mechanism commonly used in diffusion models. The variable stopping rule also enables acceleration, with the aim of producing higher-quality samples in fewer diffusion steps.

The authors apply the framework to point clouds, climate and geographical events on the Earth's sphere, unweighted graphs represented as binary matrices, and image segmentation maps with categorical entries. They report considerable improvements in both generation quality and speed over state-of-the-art approaches. The findings demonstrate the approach across substantially different kinds of output structure.
neurips-2022-first-hitting-diffusion-mod.tldr: First Hitting Diffusion Models use sample-dependent stopping times to generate continuous and structured data, with reported gains in quality and speed.

paragraphs: Biomolecular data contains relationships and geometry that are useful for machine learning, but turning raw biological records into suitable datasets can be a substantial obstacle. Graphein addresses this preparation step. It is a Python library that builds graph and surface-mesh representations of proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, and biological interaction networks.

The library retrieves data from established resources covering molecular structures, chemicals, and biological interactions. Users can specify individual preparation steps, and preprocessing utilities help prepare experimental files. This flexibility supports different choices about how biological information should be represented, while its design accommodates large protein complexes and interaction graphs.

Graphein interfaces with DGL, Jraph, PyTorch Geometric, and PyTorch3D while remaining framework agnostic through the broader Python scientific-computing ecosystem. Its outputs support machine learning as well as network, graph-theoretic, and topological analyses. The contribution is reusable infrastructure for producing analysis-ready biological datasets at scale. The authors make the code, examples, datasets, tutorials, and documentation freely available under the MIT License.
neurips-2022-graphein-a-python-library-f.tldr: Graphein turns biomolecular structures and interaction records into configurable graphs and meshes for machine learning and scientific analysis.

paragraphs: Masked autoencoders learn representations by reconstructing information hidden from their inputs. Their empirical success raises a theoretical question: why should solving this reconstruction task produce features useful for later prediction tasks? This paper investigates the role of masking itself, connecting the reconstruction objective to another major form of self-supervised learning.

The authors establish a relationship with contrastive learning in which masked autoencoders implicitly align positive pairs induced by masking. In plain terms, the training process encourages related masked views to have compatible representations. Using this connection, they develop downstream guarantees and analyze how the masking ratio affects learning, giving a theoretical account of how the pretraining task relates to later usefulness.

The same analysis identifies dimensional collapse, where the learned representation uses fewer effective dimensions. To address it, the authors introduce a Uniformity-enhanced MAE loss. They report that this objective effectively addresses the collapse issue and significantly improves results on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K. The theoretical connection therefore motivates a concrete modification to training.
neurips-2022-how-mask-matters-towards-th.tldr: A connection between masked autoencoding and contrastive learning motivates a uniformity-enhanced loss that addresses dimensional collapse and improves reported performance.

paragraphs: A robotic lower-limb prosthesis operates together with a person whose behavior can adapt to the device. This paper treats that interaction as a collaborative control problem, with symmetrical walking as the objective. Its reinforcement-learning framework represents the human and prosthesis as coupled agents and incorporates estimated human adaptation into the robot's controller.

The controller uses accessible physical measurements or features known to affect walking performance. The authors compare their collaborative approach with single-agent robot controllers and with adaptations of two existing multi-agent methods, MADDPG and COMA. These comparisons examine whether explicitly accounting for the coupled human response improves control beyond the alternative approaches considered.

The reported results show lower stage cost, peak error, and symmetry value, which the authors associate with better walking performance. The framework also learns walking tasks faster and achieves a higher learning success rate. Beyond these findings, the authors identify a possible future role in studying human-prosthesis interaction. That broader scientific use remains a potential development of the proposed framework.
neurips-2022-human-robotic-prosthesis-as.tldr: Modeling a person and robotic prosthesis as collaborating agents improves reported walking-control outcomes and learning success.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes geometric patterns in learned class representations and classifier weights after training continues beyond zero training error. The familiar characterization assumes balanced classes. This paper asks how to describe the phenomenon when classes contain different numbers of examples, using the unconstrained feature model as its theoretical setting.

The authors introduce Simplex-Encoded-Labels Interpolation, or SELI. For the unconstrained feature model with cross-entropy loss and vanishing regularization, they prove that representations and classifiers interpolate a simplex-encoded label matrix regardless of class imbalance. Their individual geometries follow the singular-value-decomposition factors of that matrix. This supplies a common characterization across imbalance levels without claiming that every class configuration has identical geometry.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support convergence toward SELI, but convergence worsens as imbalance increases. The theoretical analysis also shows that ridge regularization plays a critical role in shaping geometry when minority classes are present. Thus, the asymptotic characterization and the practical process of reaching it must be considered together when studying imbalanced learning.
neurips-2022-imbalance-trouble-revisitin.tldr: SELI characterizes neural-collapse geometry under class imbalance in a theoretical model, while experiments show that greater imbalance worsens convergence.

paragraphs: Models often lose accuracy when their test data differs from their training data. Adversarial training has been explored as a way to improve this out-of-distribution generalization by training against challenging perturbations. This paper examines how the structure of those perturbations affects the ability to handle larger changes in the data distribution.

The authors empirically find that perturbing each sample individually provides limited improvement: performance is maintained only at smaller perturbation scales in their investigation. Universal adversarial training is more robust at larger scales. This observation suggests that perturbations with shared, low-dimensional structure may better prepare models for the substantial distribution shifts encountered in out-of-distribution settings.

Motivated by that evidence, the paper proposes two adversarial-training variants with low-rank structure. Experiments on the DomainBed benchmark show that these methods outperform ordinary empirical risk minimization and sample-wise adversarial training. The findings support structured perturbations as a useful training choice in the evaluated settings, connecting the organization of the adversary to the kind of robustness being sought.
neurips-2022-improving-out-of-distributi.tldr: Two adversarial-training methods with low-rank perturbation structure improve reported DomainBed generalization over ordinary training and sample-wise adversarial training.

paragraphs: Few-shot class-incremental learning begins with well-sampled base classes and later adds new classes from only a few examples. A useful model must retain strong recognition of the base classes while learning representations that also support unfamiliar ones. Applying a classification margin during base training creates a difficult tradeoff between these two objectives.

The paper interprets this tradeoff as class-level overfitting in the patterns the model learns. Its analysis attributes the problem to a constraint for learning margin-based patterns that is too easily satisfied. Meeting that constraint can therefore leave unresolved the tension between fitting the existing classes and generalizing to classes introduced later.

The proposed method adds another constraint to pattern learning, drawing it from the margin-based patterns themselves. This makes the training objective directly address the identified source of class-level overfitting. Experiments on CIFAR100, CUB200, and miniImageNet show that the method mitigates the problem and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The contribution links the base-training margin dilemma to a specific learning mechanism and modifies that mechanism.
neurips-2022-margin-based-few-shot-class.tldr: An additional constraint on margin-based pattern learning reduces class-level overfitting and improves reported few-shot class-incremental performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from retinal activity helps reveal what visual information is present in the signals sent toward the brain. This paper develops an approximate maximum a posteriori method, combining a model of how images produce retinal responses with a separate prior describing plausible natural images. Reconstruction therefore draws on both neural evidence and image structure.

The retinal encoding component is a generalized linear model that includes dependence on a cell's spike history and on neighboring cells' spikes. The natural-image prior comes implicitly from a deep convolutional network trained to remove image noise. The authors apply this combination to simultaneously recorded spikes from hundreds of retinal ganglion cells in an ex vivo preparation.

The reconstructions match or exceed state-of-the-art perceptual similarity, show additional fine detail, and use substantially fewer model parameters than previous approaches. Replacing either component with a simpler alternative significantly reduces performance. These comparisons indicate that both the richer retinal response model and the denoiser-based image prior contribute essentially to the reported reconstruction quality.
neurips-2022-maximum-a-posteriori-natura.tldr: Combining a retinal response model with a deep-denoiser image prior produces detailed natural-image reconstructions from recorded retinal spikes.

paragraphs: Contextual Bayesian optimization selects actions repeatedly while receiving side information, such as weather conditions. In wind energy, an action could specify operating parameters. Standard approaches assume that changing the action between rounds is free, but physical adjustments can carry costs. This paper incorporates those costs into an episodic version of the decision problem.

The proposed algorithm combines randomized mirror descent with Gaussian-process confidence bounds. It builds on an online-learning approach for metrical task systems, connecting uncertainty about action performance with the expense of moving between decisions. The authors analyze regret against the offline optimal sequence within each episode, providing rigorous guarantees relative to that comparison.

The application is altitude optimization for airborne wind energy systems, where changing altitude introduces the kind of movement tradeoff the formulation captures. When movement costs are substantial, the method consistently outperforms standard contextual Bayesian optimization algorithms in the reported evaluation. The result shows why evaluating a sequence of decisions must account for the cost of transitions as well as the value of individual actions.
neurips-2022-movement-penalized-bayesian.tldr: A Bayesian optimization method accounts for costly action changes and improves reported wind-energy optimization when movement costs are substantial.

paragraphs: Sufficient dimension reduction seeks a compact representation that retains the information needed for a prediction task. Nonlinear methods can capture relationships that simpler reductions miss, but existing approaches often struggle to scale to large datasets. This paper addresses that computational obstacle with a new stochastic neural network formulated within a rigorous probabilistic framework.

The proposed network is used to perform sufficient dimension reduction on large-scale data. Its training procedure uses adaptive stochastic gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo, connecting neural-network learning with probabilistic sampling. The authors also study the algorithm's convergence rigorously, so the contribution includes analysis of the training procedure as well as the representation model itself.

Experiments cover real-world classification and regression problems. The method compares favorably with existing state-of-the-art sufficient dimension reduction approaches and is computationally more efficient on large-scale data. These findings support the proposed framework as a practical way to extract predictive information from high-dimensional inputs while addressing the scalability problem that motivates the work.
neurips-2022-nonlinear-sufficient-dimens.tldr: A probabilistic stochastic neural network provides scalable nonlinear sufficient dimension reduction with analyzed training convergence and favorable empirical results.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using an unlabeled stream encountered after training, helping it respond to distribution shifts without collecting new labels. Many existing methods assume that incoming samples are independent and identically distributed. This paper examines the more realistic possibility that nearby samples are temporally related and finds dramatic failures among most existing methods in those scenarios.

NOTE addresses this problem with two components. Instance-Aware Batch Normalization corrects normalization for out-of-distribution samples. Prediction-balanced Reservoir Sampling selects stored samples to simulate a more independent, class-balanced stream from the correlated observations. Together, these mechanisms address both how individual inputs are normalized and which observations are used during adaptation.

Evaluations include multiple datasets and real-world streams with temporal correlation. NOTE outperforms state-of-the-art adaptation methods in the non-independent setting while achieving comparable performance under the usual independent-sample assumption. The findings make the ordering and composition of test data central to adaptation design: a method that works on shuffled observations may behave very differently when observations arrive in correlated sequences.
neurips-2022-note-robust-continual-test-.tldr: NOTE combines instance-aware normalization and prediction-balanced sampling to improve continual adaptation on temporally correlated test streams.

paragraphs: Point-M2AE adapts masked autoencoding to irregular 3D point clouds. The goal is to learn useful shape representations through self-supervised reconstruction. Its encoder and decoder use pyramid architectures, allowing the network to represent both detailed local geometry and higher-level shape information as it moves across spatial scales.

The encoder reduces the number of point tokens in stages, while a multiscale masking strategy keeps visible regions consistent across those stages. The lightweight decoder progressively restores point tokens, receiving complementary information through skip connections from the encoder. During fine-tuning, local spatial attention focuses on neighboring patterns. These choices organize reconstruction from a broad view of the shape toward local details.

With the pretrained encoder frozen, a linear SVM reaches 92.9% accuracy on ModelNet40, exceeding some fully trained methods. Fine-tuning reaches 86.43% accuracy on ScanObjectNN, reported as 3.36 percentage points above the second-best method. The authors also report benefits for few-shot classification, part segmentation, and 3D object detection, supporting the usefulness of hierarchical pretraining across downstream tasks.
neurips-2022-point-m2ae-multi-scale-mask.tldr: Point-M2AE learns hierarchical 3D representations through multiscale masked reconstruction, improving reported classification and other point-cloud tasks.

paragraphs: ProtoX explains a trained reinforcement-learning agent by organizing its behavior into scenarios represented by prototype states. The aim is to make an opaque policy understandable through representative situations. A key distinction is between states that look similar and states that play a similar role in the task, since visually different situations can lead to the same action.

The method first trains an encoder with self-supervised contrastive learning. States are treated as similar when they occur close together in time and receive the same action from the original agent. An isometry layer then lets ProtoX adapt scenario similarity to the downstream task, incorporating more than visual resemblance when learning its prototypes.

ProtoX learns through behavior cloning, using imitation learning without requiring access to the environment or agent during this training process. Its objective includes prototype-shaping terms intended to improve interpretability alongside explanation fidelity. Experiments report high fidelity to the original policy and meaningful, understandable explanations. The prototypes therefore provide a behavior-based account of the agent's decisions.
neurips-2022-protox-explaining-a-reinfor.tldr: ProtoX explains a reinforcement-learning policy through representative states that capture both visual resemblance and task-relevant scenario similarity.

paragraphs: Many fairness methods require sensitive attributes such as gender or race during training, which can be unavailable because of privacy or regulatory concerns. This paper asks how to learn useful, fairer representations without observing those attributes. It uses fully unlabeled training data, while still requiring a small labeled validation set to guide learning.

The proposed method combines contrastive learning with repeated reweighting of training examples. At each iteration, weights depend on how training-example gradient directions relate to those of validation examples. The objective is to reduce the average of the top-k validation losses, directing learning toward validation examples with relatively large errors rather than relying on demographic group labels.

The authors provide a rigorous convergence result for their model. Across three datasets, the method achieves better or comparable results to state-of-the-art methods on accuracy and several fairness measures. These findings support reweighting as a way to improve fairness without demographic annotations, while the labeled validation set remains an explicit part of the method's supervision.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-fair-repres.tldr: A contrastive-learning method reweights unlabeled examples using a small labeled validation set to improve fairness without sensitive attributes.

paragraphs: Stacking self-attention layers can cause token representations to undergo rank collapse at initialization, reducing the independent information expressed across tokens. This paper investigates why that happens and how it affects the beginning of training. Its focus is the connection between the geometry of representations and the gradients needed to learn attention.

The authors show that rank collapse causes query and key gradients to vanish at initialization, hindering training. They also analyze the origin of collapse and discuss preventing it by scaling residual branches according to network depth. This ties a representational problem to an architectural adjustment that can preserve useful signal propagation through the stack.

The analysis further finds that particular architectural hyperparameters affect query, key, and value gradients differently, producing disproportionate gradient norms. The authors suggest that this imbalance helps explain the widespread use of adaptive optimization methods for transformers. That optimizer connection is an explanatory suggestion, while the central analysis directly concerns collapse, initialization, gradient behavior, and the role of residual scaling.
neurips-2022-signal-propagation-in-trans.tldr: The paper links transformer rank collapse to vanishing query and key gradients at initialization and analyzes depth-dependent residual scaling as a remedy.

paragraphs: Simple Graph Convolution is a fast alternative to deep graph models, but its use of graph connections implicitly favors homophily: linked nodes tend to be similar. Many graphs instead exhibit heterophily, where connections do not follow that pattern. This paper confirms through synthetic and real-data experiments that the original simple method is ineffective on heterophilous graphs.

The authors propose Adaptive Simple Graph Convolution, which can adjust to both homophilous and heterophilous structure. Like its predecessor, it is not a deep model, retaining speed, scalability, and interpretability. The paper also proves performance guarantees under natural synthetic data models, giving theoretical support within those modeled settings.

On a benchmark of real-world node-classification datasets, the adaptive method is often competitive with recent deep models. The authors acknowledge that deep learning frequently achieves the highest performance. Their narrower conclusion is that heterophily alone does not make a complex deep architecture necessary: adapting a simpler graph method can already address an important source of mismatch between an algorithm and graph structure.
neurips-2022-simplified-graph-convolutio.tldr: Adaptive Simple Graph Convolution handles both homophily and heterophily while often competing with deep models on node classification.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering through a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture model whose cluster means are sparse. Its main regime keeps the nonzero fraction of each mean and the sample-to-dimension ratio fixed while dimension grows without bound. Within that setting, the authors characterize the statistically optimal reconstruction error and identify when any positive correlation with the true means becomes impossible.

They separately analyze approximate message passing through its state evolution. The resulting algorithmic threshold can exceed the information-theoretic threshold, leaving a region where the data contains recoverable information but this algorithm cannot do better than random. Approximate message passing is conjectured to be optimal among polynomial-time algorithms for the task; the abstract does not establish that broader computational optimality.

The threshold expressions show how cluster count, sparsity, and sample density affect this separation. The paper also considers sub-extensive sparsity by comparing approximate message passing with sparse PCA and diagonal thresholding. Together, the results distinguish limits imposed by the available information from the performance of specific computational approaches.
neurips-2022-subspace-clustering-in-high.tldr: The paper characterizes recovery thresholds for sparse Gaussian-mixture clustering and identifies a gap between statistical possibility and approximate message passing.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks a dominant direction involving only a subset of variables. This paper focuses on recovering its support: identifying exactly which entries of the leading eigenvector are nonzero. The challenge is that the underlying matrix is unknown and the observed version contains both missing entries and noise.

The proposed algorithm uses a semidefinite-program relaxation of an l1-regularized PCA problem that is otherwise nonconvex. The authors derive sufficient conditions for exact support recovery when entries are missing uniformly at random. These conditions involve matrix incoherence, the separation between the two largest eigenvalues, the probability that an entry is observed, and the noise variance.

These are conditions under which recovery is guaranteed, rather than a claim that recovery always succeeds with incomplete data. Synthetic-data experiments validate the theoretical results, and a gene-expression application produces encouraging, meaningful results. The contribution combines a practical optimization approach with an account of how missingness, noise, and matrix structure can still permit exact identification of the relevant variables.
neurips-2022-support-recovery-in-sparse-.tldr: A semidefinite relaxation can exactly recover sparse PCA support from noisy, uniformly missing data under stated sufficient conditions.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous graphs contain multiple types of nodes and relationships, as in social and e-commerce systems. Labels may be abundant for one node type and absent for another. This creates a problem for heterogeneous graph neural networks: useful supervision exists inside the same graph, but it is attached to a different kind of node than the prediction target.

The proposed Knowledge Transfer Network moves knowledge from a labeled source node type to an unlabeled target type using the graph's relational information. Its construction follows a theoretical relationship between the distinct feature extractors used for different node types within a heterogeneous graph neural network. The module therefore connects representations that would otherwise lack a direct route for sharing supervision.

Across 18 transfer tasks, KTN improves six types of heterogeneous graph neural networks, with gains reaching 960% for inference on unlabeled node types. It also exceeds transfer-learning baselines by up to 73%. These are reported maximum improvements across the evaluations, supporting the module's usefulness across several architectures and transfer settings.
neurips-2022-zero-shot-transfer-learning.tldr: Knowledge Transfer Networks use heterogeneous-graph relationships to transfer supervision from labeled node types to types with no labels.

paragraphs: Large language models can be expensive to serve because their weights and computations consume substantial memory and processing capacity. ZeroQuant addresses this with a post-training quantization and inference pipeline. It reduces numerical precision while coordinating the compression scheme with the system that executes the compressed model.

The pipeline combines hardware-friendly, fine-grained quantization of weights and activations, affordable layer-by-layer knowledge distillation, and an optimized backend that removes quantization and dequantization overhead. The distillation component can operate without access to the original training data. This combination addresses both the accuracy consequences of lower precision and the overhead that could otherwise reduce its computational benefits.

The authors report INT8 inference with minimal accuracy impact and speedups of up to 5.19 times for BERT-style models and 4.16 times for GPT-style models relative to FP16. Combining INT4 fully connected weights with INT8 attention weights and activations reduces memory footprint threefold. Application to large open models includes a GPT-NeoX result with similar accuracy and 5.2 times better efficiency than FP16.
neurips-2022-zeroquant-efficient-and-aff.tldr: ZeroQuant combines low-precision compression, layer-wise distillation, and optimized inference to reduce transformer serving costs with limited reported accuracy impact.
